texts.orig: ABSTRACT
texts.text: ABSTRACT

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Many pneumococcal vaccines have been developed. Economic evaluation provides a framework to inform decision-making. Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) studies on 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) have been published. We introduce the concept of health economics and the basic framework for CEAs. We present a narrative literature review of recent CEA studies involving the PCV20. We also provide guidance for interpreting vaccine-related CEAs. We included 26 CEAs (17 in adults, nine in children) from 15 countries in this review. Eight of the pediatric studies and 11 of the adult studies concluded that PCV20 strategy would be cost-saving compared with existing vaccine(s), in at least one comparison. CEA is a modeling method based on existing data but includes a degree of uncertainty. It is therefore important to interpret the results of a CEA study with an understanding of the features and limitations of the analysis.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Streptococcus pneumoniae , a cause of pneumonia, may lead to invasive pneumococcal disease and death, with a heavy global mortality burden. 1 Pneumococcal infections may cause otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia and meningitis in severe cases. 1 Many new pneumococcal vaccines have been developed in recent decades. 1 , 2 There are currently two types of vaccine available: pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV). Since the release of the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23), the 7-valent PCV (PCV7), 10-valent PCV (PCV10), 13-valent PCV (PCV13), 15-valent PCV (PCV15), 20-valent PCV (PCV20), and 21-valent PCV (PCV21) have been developed and released in some countries. 3 , 4

texts.orig: For this formula, we assume that a new vaccine becomes available. After calculating the respective costs and effects for both the new vaccine and the existing vaccine, the ICER is calculated as the difference in costs divided by the difference in effects. Note that the cost here includes not only vaccine administration but also treatment of the disease and the related costs. texts.label: text
texts.orig: The central point in Figure 1 (zero) indicates the existing vaccine option. The incremental cost of the new vaccine relative to the existing vaccine is plotted on the y-axis, and the incremental effectiveness of the new vaccine relative to the comparator is plotted on the x-axis. The cost is measured in the country's currency, and QALY is widely used as the effectiveness measure. 10 , 12 The outcome of a CEA is drawn at one point (gray circle) in the cost-effectiveness plane, and the slope of the straight line between the gray circle and the central point of the figure indicates the ICER. 10–12 In Figure 1 , t the dashed line represents the cost-effectiveness threshold. The interpretation is given as follows 10–12 , 14 , 15 : if the new vaccine (gray circle) is indicated in the southeast (SE) quadrant of the graph, then it is likely to be more effective and less costly compared with the existing vaccine, and is described as "dominant." In this case, the choice between vaccines is clear. If it is plotted in the northwest (NW) quadrant, then the new vaccine is likely to be less effective and more costly compared with the existing vaccine, and the choice between the vaccines is clear, too. The northeast (NE) and southwest (SW) quadrants are "trade-off" cases; the SW offers cost savings at the expense of some health benefits, and the NE depicts a common situation in which the new vaccine is more effective, but also more costly. In the latter case, the choice as to whether the new vaccine should be included in a NIP is more difficult: the slope of the straight line from the gray circle to the center depends on both the effectiveness measure and the cost measure (Figure 1).

texts.orig: To provide guidance on whether the new vaccine is cost-effective, the cost-effectiveness threshold can be used. 11 The cost-effective -ness threshold is sometimes described as the "willingness-to-pay threshold" 14 , 15 and is the maximum amount of money that society is willing to pay for gaining 1 QALY. Using a cost-effectiveness threshold per health benefit gained, such as cost per QALY, we can consider whether the intervention – a new vaccine – is cost-effective. 11 Researchers should use local thresholds recommended in country-specific guidelines. 16 For instance, in the United Kingdom (UK), the threshold is explicit. 11 , 17 However, in the US, there is no exact threshold that is commonly recognized. 11 Moreover, many countries do not have local thresholds. In this case, a threshold that is not based on gross domestic product per capita is recommended. 11 , 14 The transparency and account of the threshold applied are crucial. 11 , 16

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As a feature of CEA, parameters are estimated and modeled using the best existing data available from different sources. 10 Also, some parameters are assumed because existing or reliable data do not exist. Therefore, the uncertainty in each parameter as well as in point estimates should be evaluated. 11 The calculation of uncer -tainty is known as sensitivity analysis. The range or level for a sensitivity analysis should be defined and the results reported in the study. 10 To specify the uncertainties, a deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) and probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) are usually undertaken. 11 In a DSA, one or more parameters are manually changed and how the results are affected by the change are then investigated. DSAs can be either one-way or multi-way: a one-way sensitivity analysis measures the impact on the results of varying a single parameter while the remainder are kept constant. A multi-way sensitivity analysis measures the impact on the results of changing the value of several parameters at the same time. In a PSA, the joint uncertainty in all parameters varies within a certain range and is input randomly and simultaneously by specifying the distributions and iterations of the model. 12 , 18 The results are then depicted as a plot of repeated numbers. 14 Figure 2 presents an example of PSA output. Scenario analysis is measures the impact on the results of varying the scenario itself in the base case. 10 , 14

texts.orig: To optimize vaccination coverage, governments plan NIPs to sustain routine immunization, and every vaccine schedule is then aligned to target population, age, and health status. 11 We therefore searched the current pneumococcal vaccination schedules for the 15 countries featured in the literature search results to capture details of the current landscape 48–58 (Table 3). Note that the schedules for routine vaccination programs varied between countries. For pediatric vaccination, PCV10 (one country), PCV13 (seven countries), PCV15 (six countries), and PCV20 (three countries) were included in current schedules (with the option to choose in some countries); however, vaccines of unknown valency in schedules were not counted. In some countries, individuals could choose the vaccine valency they wish to receive. Furthermore, the number of doses differed between countries; for example, 1 + 1, 2 + 1, 3 + 1 (where "+" represents a booster vaccine), even if the same vaccine was scheduled. For adults, PCV13 (two), PCV15 (one), PCV20 (six), PCV21 (one), and PPSV23/PPV23 (eight) were scheduled (including with the option to choose or booster vaccine). The target age stipulated in the schedule also varied in these countries (e.g., ≥65 years, or ≥60 years, or ≥75 years).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The concept of "comparison" is the basis of the study question in a CEA study. In the case of pneumococcal disease, pneumococcal vaccines with a higher valency are continually being developed. Let us assume a choice between two alternatives: a new vaccine A and an existing vaccine B. Vaccine A may be in development and existing vaccine B may be a lower-valency vaccine; thus, current standard practice(s) is often used as vaccine B. 14 Because there may be more than two possible vaccines, all relevant alternatives should be considered 10 depending on a particular country's vaccine strategy or the researcher's academic interests. A clear description regarding comparators is crucial.

texts.text: Perspective and costing

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Various decision-makers with specific interests can be assumed in each economic evaluation. 10 The perspective in CEA is directly related to the costs and consequences counted in the model, e.g., whose costs and consequence are estimated, and to what extent they are evaluated. 10 , 15 Although there are many potential decision-makers in public health programs, such as a vaccination program, health-care provider, specific payers, and societal perspectives are usually considered. 11 The choice of perspective may depend on the research purpose or research context. 11 , 14 The perspective of the research relates to the extent of costing and benefits. 14 From the perspective of a health-care provider or payer perspective, the costs directly borne by providers (such as hospitals) or by payers (such as Ministry of Health) are estimated by each. 11 From a societal perspective, the costs incurred by households, such as transportation costs, are included, as well as costs incurred by provider and payer. 11 However, those included costs are not the same from each perspective or in each study. Costs for the vaccination program are estimated by referring to guidelines indicating how to estimate these. 11 , 14

texts.orig: Discounting/discount rate
texts.text: Discounting/discount rate

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In CEA modeling, the future costs and consequences of an intervention are calculated at their present value. However, it is not possible to sum up the costs and benefits that may occur at different time points. For example, a sum of money deposited or invested now may show a return in the distant future, but an earlier benefit is preferred. This is the so-called "time preference" concept in economics. 10 In a health-care setting, although program costs occur in the present, the disease pathway can vary. Therefore, the parameter of discounting is considered in the model, depending on the specific features of the disease or intervention. Whereas vaccination programs, such as those for influenza may, have immediate short-term effects, the effectiveness of a vaccination program for pneumococcal disease may last for a relatively long time. 14 In the latter case, future costs and consequences are reduced by discounting as the benefits of the vaccination program become apparent. 10 WHO guide recommends the rate in the guideline in the country. 14 The following two analysis rates are also recommended: 3% and 0% discounting for costs and health outcomes, respectively, and 3% discounting for both costs and health outcomes. 14 Alternatively, in the absence of national guidelines, a discount rate of 3–5% would be common. 10 , 11

texts.orig: Indirect effects
texts.text: Indirect effects

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The ultimate aim of a vaccination program is to prevent vaccinated individuals from becoming infected with an infectious disease. Moreover, via vaccination, individuals can avoid acquiring infectious diseases from their surrounding environment. The spread of diseases among non-vaccinated individuals may also be reduced owing to the achievement of herd immunity. 11 , 14 As a feature of the economic evaluation of vaccination, these effects can be considered indirect effects in a CEA model. In the static model, risk reduction from herd immunity may be modeled as an effect. 11 In addition to herd immunity, the disease burden owing to factors such as serotype replacement or antimicrobial resistance can also be considered indirect effects in the model; these effects are described as indirect effects. 14

texts.text: Costs

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Costs are based on the concept of "opportunity cost," which refers to the value of what is given up by others. 10 Costs for vaccination and costs to be averted that are related to each treatment are estimated based on the disease pathway or alternatives in the model. Because the price of a vaccine that is still in development or not yet licensed is unavailable, this cost would be based on an assumption or with reference to the price of an existing vaccine. 11 Medical treatment refers to costs related to the fact that vaccines may reduce the probability of disease in the model; this information may be obtained from the literature. Therefore, it is important to state which costs are input in the model and to cite their source, as well as the rationale for using the source. 11 , 14 The vaccine price includes uncertainty if it is not known. As such, the uncertainty of costs within some ranges can be explored in several ways, such as in threshold analysis and one-way sensitivity analysis. 11 , 14

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A CEA is a model-based study that relies on the parameters input to the model. Therefore, some bias may be present in the model assumptions or parameters estimated. 11 The funding sources in economic evaluation should be reported. Among the studies reviewed herein, many (19/26) were sponsored by pharmaceutical companies, including all nine pediatric studies. Because sponsorship bias can occur in CEA studies, 63 it is important to be fully transparent regarding a study's funding source. 11

texts.text: Conclusion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In this article, we conducted a narrative literature review of recent CEA studies involving the PCV20 vaccine to provide an overview of the CEA models used and to offer guidance on how to interpret CEA studies in vaccination programs. Despite differences in the model structure and parameters with respect to the research setting in the reviewed studies, the PCV20 vaccine was relatively favorable for both pediatric and adult indications.
texts.text: In this article, we conducted a narrative literature review of recent CEA studies involving the PCV20 vaccine to provide an overview of the CEA models used and to offer guidance on how to interpret CEA studies in vaccination programs. Despite differences in the model structure and parameters with respect to the research setting in the reviewed studies, the PCV20 vaccine was relatively favorable for both pediatric and adult indications.

The results of a CEA may inform decisions regarding whether to introduce a new vaccine or replace existing vaccines in a vaccine schedule. Thus, additional CEA studies on PCVs will likely be performed and published as new, higher valencies are developed. However, as stated previously, a CEA may be variable and will contain a level of uncertainty. It is therefore important to interpret the results of a CEA study with an understanding of the features and limitations of the analysis.
